attack_mechanism: At each active permutation clock, the registered 1600-bit `out` state captures `round_out`; on a new block, the rate portion first incorporates `in ^ out[1599:1024]`. `keccak.f_permutation_.out` exposes that persistent state across absorption and round iterations. A scan read or internal probe of `keccak.f_permutation_.out` immediately after block acceptance reveals the capacity and rate state surrounding the secret input. The supporting RTL chain is `keccak.in -> keccak.padder_.in -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.e[0][0] -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_out -> keccak.f_permutation_.out`. Possession of the full sponge state bypasses the intended 512-bit output restriction and can disclose the absorbed input or chaining state.

During later `calc` cycles, the same register successively stores outputs of the two-round combinational block until the round counter completes. `keccak.f_permutation_.out` thus provides a cycle-indexed trace of the evolving permutation state. Repeated observations of `keccak.f_permutation_.out` allow an attacker to relate consecutive internal states under the known Keccak round function. The supporting RTL chain is `keccak.in -> keccak.padder_.in -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.e[0][0] -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_out -> keccak.f_permutation_.out`. The trace exposes input-dependent state transitions that are unavailable at the architectural digest interface.

On the first calculation step after `accept`, the padded rate block has just been XORed into the persistent state and is being evaluated by the two-round Keccak network. `keccak.f_permutation_.round_.ff[3][3]` is a nonlinear chi result lane; its bits are deterministic functions of the newly accepted `keccak_in` block and the previous state. Probing `keccak.f_permutation_.round_.ff[3][3]` in this early-round window exposes an internal representation before all 24 rounds have diffused the input. The supporting RTL chain is `keccak.in -> keccak.padder_.in -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.c[0][0] -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.ee[0][3] -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.ff[3][3]`. The observation leaks lane-level information about the secret input that is not present as a directly accessible architectural signal.

On subsequent `calc` cycles, feedback from the registered permutation output re-enters the same combinational round network. `keccak.f_permutation_.round_.ff[3][3]` is recomputed for later round pairs and therefore yields a time series of input-dependent values from a nonlinear chi result lane. Sampling `keccak.f_permutation_.round_.ff[3][3]` at a fixed cycle offset across repeated operations supplies aligned intermediate values for differential or correlation analysis. The supporting RTL chain is `keccak.in -> keccak.padder_.in -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.c[0][0] -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.ee[0][3] -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.ff[3][3]`. Combining those observations can recover secret-dependent relationships even when a single lane observation is insufficient to reconstruct the input.

After the final permutation, `out1` selects the upper 512 bits of `f_out` and the top-level byte-reordering network drives them onto `out` when `out_ready` is generated. `keccak.out1` is that pre-reordered digest value rather than the hidden 1600-bit state. Observing `keccak.out1` exposes the SHA-3 result; if `keccak_in` comes from a low-entropy or enumerable secret domain, an attacker can compare offline guesses against this value. The supporting RTL chain is `keccak.in -> keccak.padder_.in -> keccak.f_permutation_.round_.f[0][0] -> keccak.f_out -> keccak.out1`. The candidate enables dictionary-style disclosure of such constrained inputs, but does not by itself imply inversion of an arbitrary high-entropy preimage.
